title: HDFC Bank Paid ₹45 Crore to a State Agency to Attract Deposits. The CEO Knew.
excerpt: India's largest private lender allegedly disguised illegal payments as marketing spend. The stock has now fallen nearly 10 percent since its chairman resigned in March.
body:
HDFC Bank, the most valuable private bank in India, is staring at its deepest governance crisis in years after a report revealed that the lender paid ₹45 crore ($4.7 million) to a Maharashtra state road development corporation to attract large deposits — and that CEO Sashidhar Jagdishan was aware of the arrangement.

The Indian Express reported on Wednesday, citing internal documents and sources, that HDFC Bank routed the payments through its marketing department, disguising them as contributions to a road safety campaign run by the Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation (MSRDC). In reality, the payments were incentives designed to secure bulk government deposits — a practice that Indian banking regulations explicitly prohibit.

## What the Rules Say

The Reserve Bank of India does not allow banks to offer differential interest rates to attract deposits. Every depositor placing the same amount for the same tenure must receive the same rate. The alleged MSRDC payments effectively created a two-tier system: the official interest rate visible on paper, and a hidden incentive layer that made HDFC Bank's offer more attractive than competitors'.

This is not a technicality. Differential pricing for deposits distorts the banking system's pricing signals and creates an uneven playing field that smaller banks cannot match. If the allegations hold, HDFC Bank was essentially buying deposits through a back channel while presenting a clean face to regulators.

## The CEO's Shadow

The most damaging element of the report is the allegation that Jagdishan — whose three-year term as CEO expires in October — was personally aware of the payment arrangement. HDFC Bank has not yet submitted an application to the Reserve Bank of India for Jagdishan's reappointment. Whether the RBI will now approve a second term is an open question that the market is already pricing in.

Shares of HDFC Bank fell as much as 2.6 percent on Wednesday, trading at ₹764 in Mumbai. Since March 19, when part-time chairman Atanu Chakraborty abruptly resigned — stating that practices at the bank were "not in line" with his "personal values and ethics" — the stock has fallen 9.5 percent.

## Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

HDFC Bank is not just any Indian bank for the diaspora. It is the bank that millions of NRIs trust with their Non-Resident External (NRE) and Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) accounts. It is the institution that processes a significant share of inward remittances and the bank many NRIs recommend to family back home. A governance crisis at HDFC Bank is, in a very real sense, a governance crisis in the financial infrastructure that connects the diaspora to India.

Legal firms appointed by the bank to review the claims have yet to find material lapses, Reuters reported earlier this month. But the drip of revelations — the chairman's resignation, the Credit Suisse AT1 bond mis-selling probe, and now the MSRDC payments — has created a pattern that investors and regulators cannot ignore.

## What Happens Next

The RBI has so far maintained that it found no material governance issues at HDFC Bank following Chakraborty's departure. Governor Sanjay Malhotra has publicly backed the bank's financial fundamentals. But the MSRDC revelation adds a specific, documented allegation to what had previously been a cloud of vague concerns.

The market is watching three things: whether the RBI orders its own investigation into the MSRDC payments, whether Jagdishan's reappointment proceeds on schedule, and whether HDFC Bank's board issues a detailed public response that addresses the substance of the Indian Express report rather than offering a blanket denial.

For India's largest private lender, the question is no longer whether there is a governance problem. The question is how deep it goes.
